parole.significato: a suffix appended to words to create an agent noun, much like English -er/-or
parole.testo: Likely from Latin -ārius.

parole.significato: Forms nouns from verbs, chiefly action nouns and result nouns. Now unproductive.
parole.testo: Found suffixed exclusively to verbs loaned from Latin verbs in the first conjugation, -ō, -āre, hence likely itself borrowed from Latin -āta n pl (“-ed things”). Compare gjykatë (“court”), akin to Romanian judecată (“judgement; court”), and note also Italian -ata often used found in the same deverba
From Latin -ōnea, -ōnia, whence Romanian -oaie and Aromanian -oanji -oanje -onje.
Learned borrowing from Latin -tās, -tātis. Doublet of -tet.
From Latin abacus or Italian abaco.
Learned borrowing from Latin abdicō (“abdicate”).

It seems to be a complicated compound *a-bonus-ina, a derivation of Latin bonus with a similar development as Romanian pa bune "for real", creating the prefix a- and with an adverbial suffix -ina (Standard -irë), often used in Archaic Gheg.
Learned borrowing from Latin abrogō (“abrogate”).
Learned borrowing from Latin absolūtus.
Learned borrowing from Latin absorbeō.
Learned borrowing from Latin abstentus.
Learned borrowing from Latin abstineō (“abstain”).
Learned borrowing from Latin abstractus.
Learned borrowing from Latin absurditās.
Learned borrowing from Latin abūsus.
Learned borrowing from Latin aciditātem, accusative singular of aciditās (“sourness, acidity”), from acidus (“sour, acid”), or through French acidité. See acid.
Borrowed from Latin adamās, from Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas, “diamond”).

Borrowed from Latin adōrāre (“revere, admire, adore”) or Italian adorare (“adore”). According to Orel, it is a learned borrowing from Latin. Attested in Buzuku's Missal as adoronj (influenced by the Italian cognate), while other old authors use the popular term adhëronj.
Learned borrowing from Latin administrātiō.
Mediopassive form of active admiroj (“to admire”). Learned borrowing from Latin admīror.
Active form of mediopassive admirohem (“to be admired”). Learned borrowing from Latin admiror.
Ultimately borrowed from a derivative of Latin ad directus, from Vulgar Latin *dīrēctiāre, from Classical Latin dīrēctus (“straight”). Compare French adresse.

Borrowed from Latin āēr (“air”), ultimately derived from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”). Topalli posits Italian aria (“air”) as another possible source, considering that the Latin term is already (potentially) borrowed into Albanian as erë (“wind, air, smell”); alternatively, it is a doublet.
Modern learned borrowing from Latin acācia, from Ancient Greek ἀκακία (akakía).
Probably borrowed from Latin amiantus, ultimately from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓μῐ́ᾰντος (ămĭ́ăntos).
From amë (“source; mother; stub”) + -zë. Sense 1 is likely a calque of Latin mātrīcula (“register”).

parole.significato: to patch, mend, doctor, cobble, restore
parole.testo: Perhaps from arnë (“patch”) + -oj, ultimately a derivative of harr (“to weed”). But more likely borrowed from Latin renovāre (“to renew, restore, revive”), which is supported by the form of the aorist, as well as the more conservative spelling arënoj, which would make arnë a back-formation.
According to Çabej, a derivative of harr (“to weed”). Alternatively a back formation of arnoj (“to patch”), borrowed from Latin renovāre (“to renew, restore, revive”).

parole.significato: education (process or art of imparting knowledge, skill and judgment)
parole.testo: Gerund of arsej (“to teach, give knowledge”), from arsye (“reason”), itself a borrowing from the accusative Latin ratiōnem of Latin ratiō.
Learned borrowing from Latin ars, artem.
Learned borrowing from Latin articulus.
Borrowed from Latin asbestos, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἄσβεστος (ásbestos).
From Latin asper (“rough, uneven”).
From Latin atrophia.
Learned borrowing from Latin auctor.

parole.significato: authority (the power to enforce rules or give orders)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin auctōritās.
Borrowed from French avocat, from Latin advocātus.
From Latin barathrum (“chasm, pit, hell”), derived from Ancient Greek βάραθρον (bárathron, “gulf, cleft, pit”).
Calque of Latin cōnsonāns (or of German Mitlaut?) via bashkë- + tingëllor.
From bekoj + -im, bekoj a borrowing from Latin benedīcō.
Seemingly from Latin occurring twice; in pairs. The first element bi- ("two(fold)") also occurs in binjak.

parole.significato: A biographer (the writer of a biography).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin biographus or Ancient Greek βιογράφος (biográphos).

parole.significato: encore (brief extra performance after the main performance is complete)
parole.testo: From Latin bis (“twice; again!”).
From Latin oblāta (“shown, offered”) with various meanings, though "seal" remains an unclear development.
Borrowed from Latin brāca or brācae, likely ultimately from Proto-Germanic *brōks (> English breeches). Compare also dialectal Romanian brace, and cf. the verb îmbrăca.

A derivation of bri (“horn”), contaminated with brinjë (“rib”, literally “horn-shaped or semicircular halo over one's head”). Alternatively, it might be an irregular derivation of Latin aurora, with a strong change in pronunciation similar to Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra). The evolution could have been
Learned borrowing from Latin centuria.
Ultimately from Latin deus.
Learned borrowing from Latin debilis (“weak, frail, feeble”).
Learned borrowing from Latin delphinus.
From Latin dignus.
Calque of Latin December, from dhjetë (“ten”) + -or.
Borrowed from Latin dōnātiō. Equivalent to dhuroj + -atë.
Learned borrowing from Latin diabētēs (“siphon”).
Borrwom from Latin dignitātem. Displaced native Albanian erz.
From earlier djemënë, from Latin daemōn. Exclusive to the Gheg Catholic community.
Borrowed from Latin doctor.
Calque of Latin manualē; dorë (“hand”) + -cak.
From Latin Drivastum, although it has been noted that the accentual pattern found in Drísht < Drívastum presupposes an Adriatic "Illyrian" intermediary.
Borrowed from Latin dūrāre, with an irregular reflex of Latin -ū-.

Disputed: * From an earlier *dërkoj, from darkë. Related to ndikoj (“to pour in, to influence”) and dikoj (“to flow, to pour”). Same sense development as in derdh, with secondary meanings being "to strike down", "to cause to fall". * Borrowed from Latin indīcere (“to impose, to inflict”).
From dëshiroj or possibly Latin dēsīderium.
Calque of Latin diēs Sōlis, based on Albanian diell.
Calque of Latin diēs Lūnae, based on Albanian hënë.

Probably a calque of Latin diēs Veneris. From earlier variants e prende or e prente, from the name of Prenda, a pagan goddess protector of women, from Proto-Indo-European *prāy-, *prēy- (“to like, love”). Cognate with Proto-Germanic *Frijjō (cf. Old Norse Freyja (“lady, mistress”), English Friday),
Learned borrowing from Latin elephantem. Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἐλέφᾱς (eléphās).
Borrowed from Latin falsus (“counterfeit, false; falsehood”), perfect passive participle of fallō (“deceive”).
Learned borrowing from Latin familia; cf. Italian famiglia. Doublet of fëmijë, an older borrowing from Vulgar Latin.
Borrowed from Latin phantasma, from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma, “image, phantom”), from φαντάζω (phantázō, “to make visible”), from φαίνω (phaínō, “to cause to appear, bring to light”).
Borrowed from Latin Pharus.
Borrowed from Latin fātum. Jolk claims a derivation from Gothic fadi-.
Borrowed from Latin fīlum (“thread”).
Ultimately from Latin victoria, via a Balkan Romance language.
A formation similar to fletë and flugë. A loanword from Latin through Vulgar Latin may be plausible too, cf. facula; compare Romanian flacără, Italian fiaccola.
Uncertain. Possibly a Latin borrowing, from Latin formella (“small form”).
Derived from Latin fōrmō. Equivalent to formë + -oj.
First attested in 1555 by Buzuku. Borrowed from Latin forma (“form”). Alternative opinions opt for an Italian borrowing, though with less support.
Borrowed from Latin fortis.
It reflects an unattested *fosh that may result (irregularly as far as the anlaut is concerned) from *ftosh, the latter being a borrowing from Latin fētōsus, to fētus (“offspring”).
Unknown. Perhaps from Latin vīcīnus, related to or derived from fqinj, with a meaning of "hospitality" or "friendliness". Standard Albanian is ngushëlloj.
Ultimately from Latin thronus, from Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos).
Borrowed from Latin ventilō.
Borrowed from Latin fundus.
Borrowed from Latin furca.
Ultimately from Latin fortūna. Compare Romanian furtună, Greek φουρτούνα (fourtoúna), Turkish fırtına.
Probably a learned borrowing from Latin fūsus.
From fyt (“throat”). Influenced by and alternatively borrowed from Latin factūra (“making, manufacture”) (compare Romanian Romanian făptură (“creature, form”), Italian Italian fattura (“make”)).
Calque of Latin paenīnsula; from gati (“nearly”) + ishull (“island”) with seemingly irregular voiced -d-.
Probably a learned borrowing from Latin genius.
From Latin geōgraphia, from Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía).

parole.significato: people (a group of persons forming or belonging to a particular nation etc.)
parole.testo: From Latin gens (“id”).
From Latin gentem. Cognate to Italian gente, Spanish gente, and others.
Unknown. Possibly from Latin garrio.

parole.significato: to collect bit by bit, gather
parole.testo: From Latin collīmitāre (“to draw boundaries, *to unite”).
From Latin graecus, from Ancient Greek Γραικός (Graikós). Ultimately forms a doublet of gërk.
From Latin collūctārī, present infinitive of collūctor (“to struggle, contend”). A doublet of gulçoj.
Unknown. Maybe from Latin jūstus.
Ultimately from Latin gutta.
Borrowed from Latin cottizare, from Ancient Greek κοττίζω (kottízō).
From Latin gaudium.
Learned borrowing from Latin hepar (“liver”).

Borrowed from Latin hōra (“hour, time, season”), through Vulgar Latin with unexplained preservation of h or more likely the coincidental reappearance by other means. Cognate with Romanian oară. Doublet of orë (“hour, clock, watch”), a recent borrowing.
Learned borrowing from Latin historia.
From Latin idolum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image, idol”).
Borrowed from Latin altārium.
Learned borrowing from Latin imāginor.
Learned borrowing from Latin interpretor.
Either from a lost transitive Romance verb *iranare, from Latin ira. Otherwise a derivative of irë (“wrath, heroism”) or related to irnohem.
Ultimately from Latin Iānuārius (“January”).
From Latin ēcho, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ). Used as a basis for jehoj (“to echo”) and jehonë (“echo”).
From jeh, from Latin ēchō.
By surface analysis, jeh + -onë, but compare Latin ēchōnis, genitive singular of Latin ēchō.
Learned borrowing from Latin iustificō.
Learned borrowing from Latin candidatus.

parole.significato: jar, cruse, vessel, oil jar (most common usage)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cantharus (“large drinking vessel, tankard, pot”). According to Çabej directly from Ancient Greek κάνθαρος (kántharos, “drinking cup”).
Possibly borrowed from Latin cāpus, archaic form of cāpō (“rooster”).
Borrowed from Latin carota.
Borrowed from Latin carrūca or Italian carrozza (“carriage”) with semantic conflation with Italian carrozzina (“pram; wheelchair”).

parole.significato: hood of a cloak or raincoat
parole.testo: Plurale tantum; from Latin casula (“hooded cloak”). Doublet of kësulë.
From Latin carrus, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *karros (“wagon”).
From Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára).

Learned borrowing from Latin classis (“a class or division of the people, assembly of people, the whole body of citizens called to arms, the army, the fleet, later a class or division in general”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, shout”).
Borrowed from Latin coma (“hair”).
Learned borrowing from Latin comēta, from Ancient Greek κομήτης (komḗtēs, “long-haired”).
Ultimately from Latin commūnālis (“communal”), from commūnis (“common, shared”) + -ālis (“-al”), with influence from komunë in reference to local government.

parole.significato: municipality, a first-level administrative division of Kosovo
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin commūne.
Learned borrowing from Latin cōnsistō through English consist.
From Latin chorda (“gut, catgut”).
From Latin cichorēum ~ cichorium.
Possibly from Latin quartus.
From Latin corpus.
From older kuor(r). According to Çabej and Demiraj from a derivative of korr According to Orel from Latin chorus (“dance in a ring, harmony, harmonious motion”).
Enlargement of kudh, from Latin incus, incudem (“anvil”).

Borrowed from Latin cōgitō, through the intermediary stages of Proto-Albanian *kugitānja > *kugj(ë)tonj > *kuqtonj > kujtoj. The dialectal variant kultoj is due to a hypercorrection of the original form kujtoj. Compare Romanian cugeta, Spanish cuidar.
From Latin cucullus, via Greek κουκούλι. Doublet of kukull.
Borrowed from Latin colostrum.
Derivative of *kullumbë borrowed from Latin columba (“dove, pigeon”). The fruit is called after the bird because of its bluish colour, cf. Romanian porumbă (“sloe”) after palumbes (“dove”).
From Latin culmen.
Old borrowing from Latin compater (“godfather”), itself from com- + pater (“father”).
Borrowed from Latin cognātus. Compare Romanian cumnat, Aromanian cumnat, Dalmatian comnut.
From Latin cūnctārī (“to delay, hesitate”).
Borrowed from Latin contrā.
Borrowed from Latin computō (“to compute, reckon”).
From Old Albanian kunorë (preserved in Gheg), from Latin corōna (“garland, crown”). The sense marriage derives from Byzantine tradition.
Borrowed from Latin cōnsobrīnus (“first cousin, relation”).
From archaic kut, from Latin cubitus.

Borrowed from Latin castellum (“castle”). The modern form, ending in -ll, is influenced in part by Italian castello. Old Albanian kështjel (Buzuku) and këshqel show no Italian influence. An origin from Italian instead is unfavorable due to the -a- > -ë-, -e- > -je-, and -s- > -sh- changes, which sho
Borrowed from Latin clausura.
Ultimately from Latin Latīnus.
Borrowed from Latin litterārius (“literary”). By surface analysis, letër (“paper, letter”) + -ar or letra pl (“letters, literature”) + -ar.
From Latin līneus or līnea.

From Latin Ulpiāna, from Ulpius, the nomen gentilicium of Trajan + -ānus. Selami Pulaha states that the shift from Ulpiana to Lipjan is in accordance with early Albanian phonetic rules, and must therefore have been inhabited by Albanians to reach its current form. It has also been connected with the
From Latin lucrum (“gain, profit, wealth”). Compare also Romanian and Aromanian lucru (“thing”).
From Latin lucerna (“(oil) lamp”).
Borrowed from Latin līmāre.

Borrowed from Latin laxō, laxāre (“to let”), via its byform *lassō, *lassāre, evidenced by Romanian lăsa, Aromanian alas, dialectal Italian lassare. Many scholars also consider the possibility of a borrowing from Italian lasciare, although it is less likely due to the term's early attestation date a
From Latin Maius. Compare Aromanian maiu, Romanian mai, Greek Μάιος (Máios).
From Latin malleus. Compare Romanian mai, Italian maglio.
From Latin malleator (“hammerer”). By surface analysis, máj (“hammer”) + -tór.
Probably a learned borrowing from Latin māchina, ultimately from Doric Greek μᾱχᾰνᾱ́ (mākhănā́). Doublet of mokër.
Borrowed from Latin malum.
Borrowed from Latin mancus (“maimed, infirm”); doublet of mënk ‘one-armed’.
Borrowed from Latin (diēs) Mārtis.
Ultimately from Latin invidia.

parole.significato: man (who has just become a father)
parole.testo: Ffrom Latin maricosus.
Ultimately from Latin Mercurius.
Learned borrowing from Latin methodus, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos).
From Latin mors, mortem.
From Old Albanian mërekull, borrowed from Latin mīrāculum.
Borrowed from Latin murmurāre.

parole.significato: strong north wind, cold wind, gale
parole.testo: According to Orel, the form murrë ~ murrâ is borrowed with an assimilation of the initial b- from Latin boreanus (“Borean”), an adjectival formation of Latin boreās (“north wind”). However, this is highly improbable.
Learned borrowing from Latin musculus. Doublet of mushk or mushkull, which entered earlier through Vulgar Latin.
Derived from Latin medulla.

From Old Albanian kat (Gjon Buzuku 1499 – c. 1577), also attested as mkatë (Pjetër Budi 1566 — 1622) and mpkat (Pjetër Bogdani 1630—1689), from Latin peccātum (“sin, error, fault”). The origin of the initial nasal is unclear, yet it could either reflect the native preposition më (“in, on, at”) (earl
Borrowed from Latin mīror (“to be astonished at, marvel at, admire, be amazed at, wonder at”).

First attested in Matrënga's catechism as të mbëshuarë (“load, burden”). A prefixed form of pëshoj, a variation of the standard peshoj (“to weigh”), itself verbalized from peshë (“weight”), from Latin pēnsum (“id.”). Compare mësoj and pësoj for morphological development.
Borrowed from Latin meditari.
Borrowed from Latin nātūra.
Disputed: * Variant of dëkoj. * Borrowed from Latin indīcāre (“to impose, to inflict”).
Borrowed from Latin mātrīcula in the sense of early Medieval Latin mātrīna.
A prefixal derivative of *dëshkoj, from Latin dēspicārī (“to despise”), from dēspiciō.
From Latin ieiūnō (“to fast”); semantic development from 'to not eat' to 'to taste only'. See also Gheg ngjinoj. Ultimately a doublet of agjëroj.
Per Çabej from gur (“stone”) + -oj, literally "to stiffen, become petrified"; contaminated by gurrë for expressive reasons. For Orel from Latin incurrere (“to commit (a fault)”).
Derivative of *nokë, borrowed from Latin innocuus (“harmless, innocent”)

parole.significato: swim, swimming (act of swimming or ability to swim)
parole.testo: From a deverbal of Latin natāre, *notāre, compare Italian nuoto. A direct verbal borrowing would have regularly yielded **nëtoj instead of attested notoj, which must be a secondary derivation from the noun. Earliest attestations start with /mn/, likely due rebracketing of expressions such as i bie m
From numër, or borrowed from Latin numerō. Often replaces njeh (“id.”) in everyday speech.
Calque of Latin November, from nëntë (“nine”) + -or.
Learned borrowing from Latin offendō, from the compounding of the prefix ob- and *fendō.
Borrowed from Latin officium.
Ultimately from Latin offerō.
Borrowed from Latin hōra, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra). Doublet of herë.
Orel derives it from Latin pactō; cf. hoc pactō (“this way”), aliō pactō (“otherwise”).
Ultimately from Latin particula.
From Latin pāla (“shovel, spade”).
Borrowed from Latin pāx, pācem (“peace”).
Borrowed from Latin paradīsus.
Calque of Latin princeps, using parë.
from Latin paradisus
Borrowed from Latin poenitēre.
From Latin pignus.
Learned borrowing from Latin pēnis.
Learned borrowing from Latin perinaeum.
Related to or from Latin parentō (“to sacrifice, revenge a death”).
From a derivative of Latin pēnsō.
Ultimately from Latin pergula. Compare Italian pergola, Aromanian pergurã.
Borrowed from Latin planta (“plant”), according to Topalli (2017) who does not explain the semantic shift. Compare Venetan piantada (“plantation”) and piantareła (“row of vines”).
From Latin planca (“board, slab”).
From *plëhur, from Latin pulvis.
From po. Alternatively from Latin porrō (“then, moreover; but”), the loss of the final -r a result of the permanent unstressed position of the conjunction.
Probably from Latin praeda. Cf. also pre however.

parole.significato: prefect, particularly the governor of an Albanian county or (historical) prefecture.
parole.testo: Recent borrowing, ultimately from Latin praefectus (“one placed in charge”), from praeficere (“to place in charge”).

parole.significato: prefecture, especially (politics, historical) as a former first-level administrative division of Albania
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin praefectūra (“prefecture”), from praefectus (“prefect”) + -tura (“-ure: forming nouns”).
From Latin praeīre.
From Latin porrīna, a derivative of Latin porrum (“chives, leek”).
Ultimately from Latin prophēta, from Ancient Greek προφήτης (prophḗtēs, “one who speaks for a god”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + φημί (phēmí, “to tell”).
From Latin publica. Cf. Serbo-Croatian puk.
A secondary variant of pëllas (derived from Latin palātium), with the hypercorrect voicing of the auslaut. According to Meyer a variant of lëpozë ~ lëpizë.
From Latin palātium.
Unknown. Maybe from Latin provideo, used still in Italian expressions such as "Dio vede e provvede".

parole.significato: see!, look!, behold! (points out something with emphasis)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ecce.
Borrowed from Latin cella (“small room”); *qel + -zë (feminine suffix).
Borrowed from Latin centrum.

Uncertain. Related to or derived from Latin cēpa (likely borrowed through Vulgar Latin; compare Romanian ceapă), or Ancient Greek κάπια (kápia, “garlic”). Compare with Gheg kepë (“onion(s)”), which preserved the original /k/-sound.
From Latin centum, possibly borrowed through Vulgar Latin.
From Latin Cyprium (“copper”) with the contraction of aes.
Related to qartoj (“to quarrel”), from Latin certō (“to fight; to compete”).

Uncertain. Possibilities include: # Borrowed from a dialectal byform of Latin colostra (“beestings”), whence however the regularly derived kulloshtër (“beestings”). # A derivation from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlewH- (“to clean; to slide”), whence also Latvian slàukt (“to milk”). Given the heavily pasto
Internal development from sjell. Alternatively restored from an earlier *përqëlloj, from Latin percellāre (“to beat down”).
Borrowed from Latin regiō, regiōnem. Cf. Italian regione, Venetan rejon.
Borrowed from Latin rēgem, accusative of rex. Ultimately a doublet of rig.
From Latin rēmus.
Borrowed from Latin rīpa (“bank, shore”). Compare Romanian râpă, Aromanian arãpã (“ravine, precipice”).
From Latin ricinus.
Borrowed from Latin rēte through Vulgar Latin.
Borrowed from Latin rumpere (“to tear, to tear away”).
Ultimately from Latin rosalia (“garland festival”). Compare Romanian Rusalii (“Pentecost”).
From Latin rīmāri (“to dig, hoe”), present infinitive of rīmor/close to variant rīmō.
Only found in Greece. From Latin Romānus (“Roman”). Compare Romanian rumân, Aromanian armãn, Istro-Romanian rumăr.
Learned borrowing from Latin sacrificō; sakrificë (“sacrifice”) + oj (“I”).
Internationalism. Ultimately from Latin satira, satura.

parole.significato: coarse linen fabric spread on the floor
parole.testo: From Latin sagum (“sagum, cloak made of coarse fabric”).
Borrowed from Latin saeculum.
From Latin examen
borrowed from Latin syrinx, from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx)
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin scāla.
From an earlier skollë attested in Arbëresh, from Latin schola through Vulgar Latin, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ).
From Latin scortea (“made of fur or hide”) via Vulgar Latin. Compare Aromanian shcoarci, Romanian scoarță, Italian scorza. Doublet of skorcë.

* From sh- (“off”) + kruaj (“to scratch”) q.v.; for sense development, compare English write from Old English wrītan (“to incise, engrave”). The noun form shkrim was probably influenced by Latin scrībō (“write”). * From earlier shkruon (“he/she writes”), from Proto-Albanian *śkrɔ̄n < *śkrə.on < *śkr
Probably a formation from qelq (“glass”) with mobile sh-, from Latin calix.
From Latin solum.
From Latin socia.
From Latin spissus (“thick”) (cf. Italian spesso (“id.”)). Also compare Aromanian spes (“id.”).
Borrowed from Latin spīna.
Borrowed from Latin spiritus.
Borrowed from Latin explico. Compare Italian spiegare.
From Latin sporta (“basket, sieve”), contaminated with the preterite forms of shpie (“to carry”) and its derivatives (cf. shpurë and shpjertë).
From shpresë + -oj. Oryol claims a borrowing from Latin spērāre, noting the variant shpërej.
From Latin sperans, sperantia, from spero (“hope”). Compare Albanian shpërej "to hope" (doublet of shpresoj, itself from shpresë) from Latin sperāre.
From Latin spodium. Lent Romanian spuză and Aromanian spuzã.

Compound of shqip + -oj (“I”) (active voice personal suffix). Origin of shqip is disputed: * Petar Skok suggested that shqip originated from Scupi (Shkup), the capital of the Roman province of Dardania (today's Skopje). * Also claimed as from Latin excipere;, a compound of Latin ex- + capiō (“to tak
From Latin scōpa (“branch (of plant); broom”). Compare regional Italian scopiglio (“heather”).
Borrowed from Latin scūtum (“shield”).
Calque of Latin September, from shtatë (“seven”) + -or.
Singularized plural of *shtat, from Latin stātus. Per Matasović a borrowing from Italian stato.
From dialectal shtilë, with apheresis from Latin hastīle.
Borrowed from Latin strātum. Compare Romanian strat.

parole.significato: Shtriga, a vampiric witch in traditional Albanian folklore
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin strīga (“evil spirit”), from strix (“screech owl”), from Ancient Greek στρίξ (stríx). See Romanian strigoi.
From Latin stringō.
from Latin Saturnus
Probably borrowed from Latin stuppa, from Ancient Greek στύππη (stúppē). Compare Romanian stupă.
From earlier *shturrë, borrowed from Latin sturnus.
Variant of shtëroj, influenced by shter. Alternatively from Latin extenuāre.

* Orel propeses a borrowing from Latin subjugāre, with the loss of two intervocalic voiced stops. * Possibly a derivative of shuj (“to be silent, to hush”), thus originally meaning to 'bring to silence, to suppress', cognate to Ancient Greek σβέννυμι (sbénnumi, “to quench”).
From Old Albanian shëkroj, from Latin sacrō.
Borrowed from Latin summum.
An early borrowing from Latin sorbus. Synonym survë is from Greek σουρβιά (sourviá), itself also from Latin.
From Latin surdus with the native -ër/-ën suffix.
From *shush, possibly based on Latin exossus (“boneless, devoid of bones”).

From shën + Dhimitër, a calque of Latin Sanctus Demetrius, the latter derived directly from Ancient Greek Δημήτριος (Dēmḗtrios). The martyr is venerated in Albania on 26 October, linking the month to the saint's day.
From Latin sincerus.
Learned borrowing from Latin sinus. Doublet of gji.
Ultimately from Latin accipiter (“hawk”). Initial sk- influenced by shqiponjë.
Learned borrowing from Latin scrōtum.
a combination of Latin dis- and Proto-Albanian *ka-, from Proto-Indo-European *ko-.
Ultimately from Latin hospitalis (“hospice, shelter, guesthouse”). Most likely a later borrowing.
With vowel metathesis from Latin scutella (“drinking bowl, salver”) or scutula (“square dish, platter”), diminutives of scutra (“shallow pan, dish”).
Unclear. Maybe a late irregular borrowing from Latin stationem.
Ultimately from Latin traiectōrium.
Internationalism, compare German Text, French texte, ultimately from Latin textus.
Borrowed from Latin templum.
From Latin tinea.
Calque of Latin Octōber, from tetë (“eight”) + -or.
Borrowed from Latin thēsaurus, reinterpreted as thes (“sack”) + ar (“gold”).
Alteration of fjeshtër (Arbëreshë), borrowed from Latin filiaster (“step-son”).
Unknown. Proposed etymologies include: # A derivative of thellë (“deep”), as a color adjective. # From an unattested variant of Latin fulica (“coot”).
From Latin tegminem (“cover”), from tegimen, thus an ultimate doublet of tog and related to toger.
From Latin tinca.
From Latin tina (“wine vessel”).
From Latin tēgula.
According to Jokl, Tagliavini, Çabej a cognate to Proto-Slavic *mora (“nightmare”) / Ancient Greek μέριμνα (mérimna, “trouble, thought, uneasiness”). According to Orel borrowed from Latin timōrem.
From Latin torculum (“wine- or oil-press”).
Ultimately from Latin turta. Perhaps borrowed via Italian torta. Compare Romanian turtă.
From Latin tortum (“rope (for tortures)”), also in Romanian tort (“yarn, thread”).
From Latin trabem (“beam”).
From Latin traditor, from tradere (“hand over, give up, deliver”).
Ultimately from Latin trādō. Compare Romanian trăda.
Borrowed from Latin tractāre.
Probably from Latin tractus, through Dalmatian *traito.
Learned borrowing from Latin transfero, transferre (“to transfer”), from trans (“over”) and ferre (“bring”).

parole.significato: to inherit (property or something else by will)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin trānsigō (“to settle a difference or dispute, come to an understanding”), from trāns- + agō.
From Latin trīna. Compare Italian trina.
From Latin tristis.
From Latin tructa.

A variant of truaj or a derivative of terë, which explains the plural troje. Alternatively, Orel relates it to Latin trībulum (“thresher”), but the connection between 'thresher' and 'estate' is not explained.
From Latin truncus.

parole.significato: to steal from a holy site, shrine
parole.testo: From Latin *triumphiscālia
From Latin tufa. Compare Romanian tufă, Aromanian tufã.
Borrowed from Latin turma. Compare Italian torma, Romanian turmă.
From Latin turpis.
From Latin turrem (“tower”).
Probably borrowed from Latin turtur.
Borrowed from Latin turbāre (“to ruffle, to agitate”).
Borrowed from Latin trifolium.
Borrowed from Latin trifolia < trifolium. Compare Aromanian tãrfoyi.
Borrowed from Latin trifurcus.
From Old Albanian terëmet, borrowed from Latin terrae mōtus, an archaic borrowing considering the /oː/ → /e/ shift. Borrowed from Romance in its /o/ variants.
From Latin oleaster (“olive tree”).
From Old Gheg *ullin (modern ullî), with secondary -n, borrowed from Latin olīvus; expected form lli is preserved in Arvanitic.
From Latin uncāre (“to roar (of bears)”) with a secondary inlaut -r-.
Directly or ultimately from Latin ūrīna.
From Latin ōrō. Compare Romanian ura.
From Latin horreō (“to be afraid”); change in meaning also in Romanian urî (“to hate”).
Learned borrowing from Latin vagina.

Likely borrowed from Latin vallis. The term may be an example of an ancient borrowing that later fell out of use. Its presence is minimal but scattered both in Southern and Northern Albanian toponyms.
Possibly from Latin virgō (“virgin”), or related to the compound Greek (Hes.) βάριχοι ἄρνες (várichoi árnes).
Borrowed from Latin vēlum.
Borrowed from Latin opera (“id”).
Derived from Latin vitium.

parole.significato: European black pine, black pine (Pinus nigra)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abiegnus, from abies (“silver fir”).
From Latin vīctuālia (“victuals”).
Collective form of *vigjë, a hypercorrect form of *viqë, borrowed from Latin vicia.

A case of a loaned verb being suppleted by inherited forms. From Old Albanian vinj (“to come”), vjen (“he comes”), borrowed from Latin veniō. The past forms in erdh- are from Proto-Indo-European *h₁erǵʰ- and cognate with Ancient Greek ἔρχομαι (érkhomai).
From Latin via.
From Latin virgo, virginem. Compare also Romanian vergură.
From Old Albanian vërtyt, borrowed from Latin virtūtem (“virtue”).
Borrowed from Latin valēre (“to be able, to be healthy”).
From Latin versus (“verse”).

A derivative of vjet (“last year”), variant of vit (“year”), from Proto-Albanian *weta, from Proto-Indo-European *wétos (“year”), contaminated with Latin vetus, veteris. Compare Lithuanian vẽtušas (“old”, archaic), Old Church Slavonic ветъхъ (vetŭxŭ, “old, ancient”). Attributed directly to Latin vet
Attested in third person singular as vëljen (Matrënga), vien (Buzuku), vëjen (Bogdani). Borrowed from Latin valeō (“to be well, to be strong, to be worth”).
Borrowed from Latin valor, valōrem (“value”).

parole.significato: small strip, bed, patch of cultivated land
parole.testo: The forms in -anjë, -âjë arose by singularisation of the plurals of the forms in -â. Unclear, connected by Topalli (2017) to llaj (“to feed, fill up”), referring to when rain fills up the earth, by Çabej SEFSH [1950s–1980] to vëllâ (“heat wave”), considering a possible semantic parallel in the synon
From Latin venenum (“potion, poison”).
Tosk variant of old Gheg vëner, vënen, from Latin venenum.
From Latin verriculum.
From Latin voluntātem.
Borrowed from Latin volūmen (“book, roll”), from volvō (“roll, turn about”).
From Latin vēritās, vēritātem.
Borrowed from Latin vestīgō.
Borrowed from Latin unctura. Compare Romanian untură and Aromanian umturã.

Identical to and derived from zë (“voice”), with a sense development motivated by the main characteristic of these mythological figures. The term might have been contaminated with Latin Diāna (compare Romanian zână, Aromanian dzãnã, Asturian xana, Sardinian giàna). Another hypothesis, given her char
Borrowed from Latin scabiēs, compare Romanian zgaibă, Aromanian zgaibã. For the initial consonant cluster, compare zgjyrë alongside Romanian zgură from Latin scōria.
Borrowed from Latin scōria.
From Latin saburra (“sand ballast”), another variant is shur.
Borrowed from Latin aestimō.

From Latin aptus. Alternatively but less likely from Proto-Albanian *aweita, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁- (compare Ancient Greek ἀυτμή (autmḗ, “breath”), Welsh awel (“breeze”)), meaning 'to have will, have power or breath to do something'.

parole.significato: at, beside, by, near, nearby, near to, next to
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *apsera or *asper(a), perhaps representing a contamination of *aps, reflected in Ancient Greek ἄψ (áps, “backwards”), a variant of Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“off, away”), with Proto-Indo-European *h₂épero-. Cognate to Sanskrit अपर (ápara, “posterior, later, following”), Gothic

First attested in Buzuku as engjënonj with a prothetic (e)n-, then variously attested as angjinonj (Budi), me ngjinuem (Bardhi), me anjënuem (Kuvendi i Arbënit). A formation based on e(n) privative + gjër, Tosk variant of gjanë, literally “without food” (cf. esëll, egjëll). Alternatively a borrowing

Hamp suggests a connection with rri (“stand”) (see related mbërrij (“arrive”). Alternatively from Early Medieval Latin adrīpāre, derived from Latin ad (“to”) + rīpa (“shore”). Compare Italian arrivare.

From an earlier *rrësye, rendered as masculine arsye (definite singular arseu, indefinite plural arsenje) in Buzuku and feminine arrësye in Budi; from Latin ratiōnem (“reason”). Latin ō > Albanian e is regular in older borrowings, developing into -ye when followed by a syllabic consonant. The initia

parole.significato: wood splinter; chip, fragment of shell, shard, etc.
parole.testo: Perhaps from Proto-Albanian *a(k)škā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- (“axis”). Alternatively, a borrowing from Late Latin ascla, from Latin assula. Compare Romanian așchie.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin vallum. Alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“to turn, wind, roll”).

parole.significato: to rock the boat, cause to fall
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin battuō or possibly from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic. Compare Welsh bathu (“beat”); Old English beadu (“battle”)

From Proto-Albanian *mlē(n-), from Proto-Indo-European *melh₁- (“to crush, grind”). Cognate to Old Church Slavonic млѣти (mlěti, “to grind”). Alternatively, according to Orel, from Latin molere (“to grind”), with the same buccalization of m before l as seen in bletë from melitta, though note that ot
Either borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin buxus, or from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH (“to grow”) (compare Dutch bos (“woods”), English bush).
Uncertain. * Probably from Vulgar Latin *indictō from Latin indicō, or alternatively from Latin dētegō. * Alternatively from formation of dë- and ftoj, from Ancient Greek φοτίλω (photílō)
From *dromoj, a derivative of dromcë. Alternatively from Vulgar Latin *dērāmō, from Latin rāmus. Compare Romanian dărâma and Dalmatian dramur.
From Proto-Albanian *ōd-r-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- (“to smell, stink”). Alternatively, from Latin āēr.
Either from a Dalmatian reflex of Latin faciēs (“face, side”), or a derivative of fërkoj (“to rub”), or fal, from earlier Proto-Albanian *falkoj.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *fēdes, from Latin fidēs. The Vulgar Latin form is alternatively reconstructed as Vulgar Latin *fe.des.

From Proto-Albanian *spelnā, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pel- (“to say aloud, recite”); compare English spell, Armenian առասպել (aṙaspel, “myth; legend”), and possibly Ancient Greek ἀπειλή (apeilḗ, “threat”). Related to flas (“to speak”). Alternatively, possibly borrowed from Latin fābella.

Orel proposes a back-formation from fluturoj (“to fly; go fast”), from a Vulgar Latin *fluctulāre, from Latin fluctuare. Alternatively, the word could come from Proto-Albanian *flugtur, forming a group of words together with fletë, flatër, flegër, flugë. The word may have been borrowed into Romanian

parole.significato: exultation, liveliness, happiness, gaiety, merriment, mirth, joy, glee, cheer
parole.testo: From gaz or from a Vulgar Latin root *gaudimentum, from Latin gaudium or from Ancient Greek Γάϊος (Gáïos) / Latin Gaius / Latin Cāius, Ancient Greek γαίω (gaíō, “rejoice, exult”) & Ancient Greek ἄσμενος (ásmenos, “well-pleased, glad, happy, content, joyful”).
From Proto-Indo-European *geli-, *glī- (“mous”). Compare Ancient Greek γαλέη (galéē, “weasel, marten”), Latin glīs (“dormouse”). Alternatively from Latin glīrem.
Either borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin jūdicata, or a suffixed form of gjykoj; gjykoj + -atë. Compare Romanian judecată.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin gemō. Alternatively from Latin clāmāre (“to cry, shout”) with voicing of the initial group cl- (see dialectal variant glëmoj).

Back-formation of earlier *gjamët(ë), Buzuku gjamënë, (originally a neuter noun but interpreted as feminine plural), through Vulgar Latin from Latin gemitum (“groan, lamentation”). Compare Romanian geamăt. Alternatively a deverbative of gjëmoj.
Either related to krip (“hair”) (cf. krife), or borrowed from a Vulgar Latin *gripsa (compare Friulian grip (“nuthatch”)), from Latin gryps (“griffon”), from Ancient Greek γρύψ (grúps).
From an unattested *het, from Proto-Albanian *skaita, close to Lithuanian skaitýti (“to read”). Alternatively from Latin ēdictāre (“to announce”).

A derivative of kafshë + -oj. Alternatively (according to Meyer-Lübke) borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Late Latin captiō, from Latin captō. Other Latin proposals include Late Latin capsāre (Meyer) and most recently Late Latin capissere by Oryol. Given the two forms, dialectal ajsonj and Old Tosk
Either from Latin cappellus (“hat”) or its derivative Italian cappello (via the feminine cappella).
Borrowed from Latin capitulum. Alternatively, borrowed from Italian capitolo, or even an older form of capitulo.
Borrowed from Latin clupea, via dissimilation and methatesis. Alternatively from Proto-Slavic *kъlbь.

Borrowed from Latin conventum (“assembly, convention”). The plurale tantum kuvíse has been influenced by the alternation vís ~ vénd, or alternatively continuing a Vulgar Latin *conventiae. Cognate with Aromanian cuvendã, Romanian cuvânt (“word”) and Greek κουβέντα (kouvénta, “conversation; word, phr

parole.significato: goat or sheep with backward-curling horns
parole.testo: Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin cornūtus (“horned”) or alternatively from early Romanian cornută, nominative feminine of Romanian cornut.

Singularized plural of earlier *leg, *lig. Either borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin lēx, lēgem (“law”) (compare Romanian lege), from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- (“to collect, to speak”), or from the same root of Lithuanian lygùs (“equal”) and Old Prussian līgan (“court”), as substantiated by li

parole.motivo_incerta: disputed; Probably; perhaps; alternatively; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Disputed. Perhaps: * Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewH-. Cognates would include Latin luō (“to expiate, pay”), Ancient Greek λύω (lúō, “to release, untie”), Sanskrit लून (lūna), and English loose. * Alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ-o-. * More likely, an early borrowing from La
From luftë + -tar, or possibly borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin luctator, luctatōrem. Compare Romanian luptător.

parole.significato: debris (carried by river); mountain ravine, precipice
parole.testo: From Latin lustrum (“bog, morass”). Alternatively from Proto-Albanian *lūm(i)štrā, a formation based on lym.
From Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to think; mind”). Alternatively, though less likely, Orel claims a borrowing from Latin mentem (“mind”), ultimately from the same Indo-European root.
From Latin menta, or from the same Mediterranean Pre-Greek source as Ancient Greek μίνθη (mínthē).

From Proto-Albanian *mālā, akin to Ancient Greek μῆλον (mêlon, “apple”), Latin mālum (“apple”), either a cognate or borrowed from either of the two. Likely from a western dialect borrowed from Doric Greek. A borrowing from Latin would be unusually early, as the shift from *ā to o, characteristic of

Probably borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin mania (compare Romanian mânie). Alternatively from Greek μανία (manía, “madness”) given the corresponding stress. Note Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to change, exchange”). Compare Sanskrit मेनि (mení, “revenge, vengeance”), Avestan 𐬨𐬀𐬉𐬥𐬌 (maēni, “punis

From *ndërr, from Proto-Albanian *anteros, from Proto-Indo-European *an-2 (“there, on the other side”). Cognate to Old Prussian antars, anters (“other, second”), Lithuanian añtras and Old High German andar (“other”). Alternatively, from Latin alterō with irregular change of the sonorant.
Either formed from the adjective ngushtë or borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin angustāre.

Singularized plural of *nusë, from Proto-Albanian *nutjā, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)nubʰ-tyeh₂, from *snewbʰ-; compare Latin nūbō (“to marry a man”), Czech snoubiti (“to woo”). For the sense development, Greek νύφη (nýfi, “bride, daughter-in-law”), from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “bride”). Alte
Borrowed from a Romance language; cf. Italian offerta, or from Late Latin offerta, ultimately from Latin offerō.
Ultimately from Latin pācāre. Source language is uncertain, as is the possibility of a direct borrowing. Possibly from Italian pagare or alternatively a derivative of pagë, also from Italian.

* From Proto-Albanian *petja, from Proto-Indo-European *petino-, from *pet- (“to spread out, to extend”) (compare English fathom). Alternatively from Latin pannus (“cloth, rag, garment”); cf. Greek πανί (paní). * From Proto-Albanian *pena-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)penh₁- (“to draw”).

Highly disputed etymology. * either from perëndi, or Prenda. according to Durham, a sun-cult influence by Mithraism during early Roman Christianity similar Middle Greek ὁ ήλιος βασιλεύει * from Latin parento * or from Latin imperator, but this is challenging due to the existence of mbret
Borrowed from Ancient Greek περίοδος (períodos) or from Latin periodus.
From earlier pjepënë, either from Latin pepō, peponem through Vulgar Latin *pepinem or directly from Ancient Greek πέπων (pépōn, “ripe”). Compare also Romanian pepene, Aromanian piponj, peapini.

From Ancient Greek κεράσιον (kerásion, “cherry”), from κερασός (kerasós, “bird cherry”). Alternatively possibly partly through Vulgar Latin and Late Latin ceresia, from Latin ceresium, from the same Greek root. Compare Romanian cireașă, Aromanian cireashi.

Unclear; from Proto-Albanian *kertsula, possibly borrowed from Latin cercellus, circellus (“small ring, hoop”), ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek κίρκος (kírkos, “ring”). Doublet of qark, qarkull. Alternatively inherited from Proto-Indo-European *ker-ḱ- or *kert- (“to turn, to bind”), or simply
From Proto-Albanian *kai. Alternatively or more likely from Latin quī.

Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *aeramem m, whence also Italian rame, from Latin aeramen n. The variant ram reflects the variant Vulgar Latin *aeramum m, whence also Sicilian ramu, Venetan ramo, while Tosk rëm can reflect either forms.

From Proto-Albanian *(h)eríja- 'of this time, from this time, presently, of now > new, recent', a derivative of Alb. herë '(one) time, hour' etc., which is an old loan-word from Latin hōra 'time, hour' etc.; the Albanian substantive is historically not compatible with a reconstruction Proto-Indo-Eur

A term with multiple plausible etymologies. Either from Latin rāpum (“turnip”), Ancient Greek ῥάπυς (rhápus, “turnip”), or Proto-Slavic *rěpa (“turnip, beet”), or natively from Proto-Indo-European *(s)rā́ps. First attested as rrap, producing the contemporary form through plural metaphony and the Arb

Uncertain. Either: # a prefixed formation of rrë- + *fanë, with the latter unattested; from Proto-Albanian *span(d)ā, cognate to Old Norse fanta, fattr (“curved”), Latin pandus (“bend, crooked, curved”), # according to Orel, derived from rrëfej in its unattested meaning '*to carry (away)', continuin

parole.significato: Ragusa (former name of Dubrovnik: a port city in southern Croatia, on the Adriatic Sea)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *rāguša Compare Sicilian Ragusa. Alternatively from Latin Ragusium. Regarded as a quite early loanword as the /ɡ/ is dropped, a pattern in older loanwords such as mjeshtër from magister, Drisht from Drivastum, mjek from medicus, and pyll from palūs, palūdem.
Borrowed from Latin secundus directly or from Italian secondo.

parole.significato: female gown (made of wool, covering the shoulders and the chest)
parole.testo: Either from Proto-Germanic *sarkiz (“shirt, armour, hauberk”), via Gothic or from Proto-Slavic *sorka (“shirt”). Schuhard and Meyer claim a borrowing from either Latin serica or Latin sarica.

Compare Hittite [Term?] (/⁠šarra⁠/, “break, rupture, divide”), Latin serra (“id”), Lithuanian sėris (“filament”). Alternatively borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin serra; compare Aromanian sharã.

Unclear. Either from the same root as Ancient Greek σκορπίος (skorpíos), Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-, or from shkrep, since scorpions are usually found on rocks. Alternatively a borrowing from Latin scorpiō.

According to Guillaume Bonnet, possibly from Proto-Germanic *skurtaz. Alternatively borrowed from reconstructed Vulgar Latin *excurtus (cf. Italian scurto, Romanian scurt, Aromanian shcurtu), derivative of Latin curtus. The Albanian, (reconstructed) Latin, and Germanic terms developed in the same wa
From shkurt + -oj; hence shkurtoj (“to cut; make short”). Alternatively borrowed from Late Latin excurtō, from Latin curtō; cf. Romanian scurta, Aromanian shcurtedz.
Either a prefixal derivative of laj or borrowed from Vulgar Latin *experlavāre, from Late Latin perlavāre, from Latin lavō. Compare Romanian spăla, Aromanian aspel.

From Vulgar Latin *expedītāre, from Latin expedīre (“to entrict, disengage”). Alternatively, a verbal formation with a prefix denoting the movement away from something from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to spread out; to fly”), connected to pjetë (“upwards”).

From Proto-Albanian *štramba, close to Old Prussian strambo (“stubble”), Lithuanian strampas (“club, truncheon”), and Proto-Germanic *strambaz, in Norwegian dial, stramb (“strong smell”), Middle Low German stram (“strong, powerful”). Alternatively a derivative of Vulgar Latin *strambus, from Latin s

From Proto-Albanian *stūlā- or *stūlwā-, from Proto-Indo-European *stuh₂-l-eh₂ < *steh₂- (“to stand up”). Compare Ancient Greek στῦλος (stûlos), Proto-Slavic *stъlbъ (“post, pillar”). Alternatively from Byzantine Greek στῦλος (stûlos) or from Latin stilus (“stake, spike”) .

From Proto-Albanian *tˢ́ika, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *ćīkā ~ *ćeykā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱeh₃- (“to sharpen”). A PPA form *ćīkā supports a Proto-Indo-European *k̑iH-keh2- form, while *ćeykā supports a Proto-Indo-European *k̑éi̯H-keh2- form. The absence of an a-umlaut favors against a short -i-
Either from Proto-Albanian *wa(d), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₂dʰ- (“to go, walk”), or from Latin vadum; impossible to determine. Possibly forms a doublet of vete.
Possibly from Latin iānua (“door, entrance”), prefixed with z-. Alternatively related to gëloj (“to burst out”). Çabej analyses a possible older form of Proto-Albanian *glon-.
Possibly from Latin usūra. Alternatively borrowed from Ottoman Turkish [script needed] (yzër).
